clue.text: SOB I summon turned up in auto

parts.note: an SOB is a rotter, a cad

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the word for summon is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to summon someone is to call them

explanation.surface: Someone cursing a summons that was flipped over inside a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' reverses CALL to LLAC beneath CAD and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Auto is American for a car, and this is a famous American luxury car make.

clue.text: Extremely aware of social injustice acceptable in cowboy country

indicators.note: in says the word for acceptable sits inside the cowboy region

parts.note: the American West is the land of cowboys
acceptable means OK

explanation.surface: Social awareness turning up somewhere unexpected, among cowboys.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlative of the slang adjective for being alert to social injustice, so most aware.

clue.text: Regret having overturned launch carrying article from this part of world

indicators.note: in a down clue, overturned means the word for regret is read upwards

parts.note: to regret is to rue

indicators.note: carrying means the word for launch holds the article within it

parts.note: to launch a business is to open it
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A sorry tale of a launch going wrong somewhere in the region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturned' makes RUE into EUR; OPEN carrying A gives OPEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for someone or something belonging to the continent where the setter's paper is printed.

clue.text: John translated for English poet, turning up on time

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it
in a down clue, turning up means the poet's name is read upwards

parts.note: T. S. Eliot, the poet who took British citizenship

explanation.surface: Someone translating poetry for an English poet, arriving punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' is American slang for a lavatory; the definition asks for the British word. ELIOT reversed gives TOILE.
explanation.definitionFit: The American slang word for a lavatory, rendered into British usage, is this common word for it.

clue.text: Racket having undergone extraction of uranium in US

definitions.text: Racket having undergone extraction of uranium in US

parts.words: Racket having undergone extraction of uranium in US
parts.note: the British word for a din loses its U (uranium's symbol) in American spelling

explanation.surface: A noisy mining operation taking uranium out somewhere in America.
explanation.walkthrough: American spelling drops the U that British spelling keeps in words like this one; U is the chemical symbol for uranium.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a loud noise or uproar, and this is the American spelling of that word.

clue.text: Put in enclosure or apprehend, having changed sides throughout

indicators.note: sides are left and right, so every L becomes R and every R becomes L in the word for apprehend

parts.note: to apprehend a suspect is to collar them

explanation.surface: Choosing whether to pen something in or arrest it, after switching allegiance.
explanation.walkthrough: L (left) and R (right) swap places all through COLLAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To pen livestock in a fenced area is the ranching verb for confining them.

clue.text: Comedy that has elite doubled up in London, not New York

definitions.text: Comedy that has elite doubled up in London, not New York

parts.words: Comedy that has elite doubled up in London, not New York
parts.note: U means upper-class or elite; the British spelling of the word for comedy has two Us, the American one only one

explanation.surface: A comedy show with doubled-up elites playing in London rather than New York.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the convention for upper-class (elite); British spelling carries a second U that American spelling omits.
explanation.definitionFit: Comedy and funniness are synonyms, and the British spelling is the one with two Us.

clue.text: Less sensible ingredient of English breakfast

definitions.meaning: a slice of bacon, a staple of the British cooked breakfast

explanation.surface: A comment on the folly of eating a full fry-up.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of a word for reckless, and also a slice of bacon served at breakfast.

clue.text: Main area separating Yanks and Limeys

definitions.text: Main area separating Yanks and Limeys

parts.words: Main area separating Yanks and Limeys
parts.note: the main is the sea; the ocean between Americans (Yanks) and Britons (Limeys)

explanation.surface: A boundary or region that keeps Americans and Britons apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like 'chief' but is the old poetic word for the open sea. Limeys is American slang for Britons.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocean lying between North America and Britain is the body of water described.

clue.text: Relaxing holiday for American Oscar winner

definitions.meaning: a leisurely sea voyage taken as a holiday
Tom ..., the American film star given an honorary Oscar

explanation.surface: A restful break arranged for a film star.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a holiday on a ship and the surname of a famous American actor.

clue.text: Missing part of garment for Friar Tuck or Robin? Not so

definitions.text: Missing part of garment for Friar Tuck or Robin? Not so

parts.words: Missing part of garment for Friar Tuck or Robin? Not so
parts.note: lacking the head covering of a cloak; Robin Hood is literally not without his Hood

explanation.surface: Wondering whether Friar Tuck or Robin has lost part of a cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: The friar's habit has a cowl, and Robin's surname is Hood, so neither of them lacks one.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective meaning lacking the head covering attached to a garment.

clue.text: Trouble after judge shortened sentence to clink

indicators.note: after places the word for trouble behind the judge's letter

parts.note: J is the abbreviation of judge
to trouble someone is to ail them

explanation.surface: A judge cutting short a sentence, causing trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Clink is slang for prison, so sentencing someone to it is the verb for imprisoning.

clue.text: Heard about a British undergarment being misrepresented

indicators.note: about means the word for heard goes around the other pieces

parts.note: a court has heard a case when it has tried it
a vest is a British undershirt (an American vest is a waistcoat)

explanation.surface: Gossip about a British vest getting the wrong story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' suggests sound, but here it is a legal case heard, i.e. TRIED. In Britain a vest is an undershirt, not a waistcoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Past participle of a verb meaning to parody or distort, so having been misrepresented.

clue.text: United States and Queen Elizabeth II, for example

definitions.text: United States and Queen Elizabeth II, for example

parts.words: United States and Queen Elizabeth II, for example
parts.note: SS United States and the QE2 were famous transatlantic passenger ships

explanation.surface: Naming a nation and a monarch as examples of something.
explanation.walkthrough: These read as a country and a queen, but both are names of great passenger ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Two famous ships of the type that carried passengers across the sea.

clue.text: From a large kind of yacht endlessly make fun of infamous island

parts.note: L is the clothing abbreviation for large
a cat is a catamaran, a twin-hulled yacht

indicators.note: endlessly means the word for make fun of loses its last letter

parts.note: to razz someone is to tease them

explanation.surface: Mocking a notorious island from aboard a big catamaran.
explanation.definitionFit: The San Francisco Bay island that held a notorious federal prison.

clue.text: Defining characteristic of King George's head, in fact

indicators.note: in places George's initial inside the word for fact

parts.note: fact and reality are synonyms

indicators.note: head picks the first letter of George's

explanation.surface: A remark on what really defines King George.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King George' reads as one name, but King belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal status or kingliness is what defines a monarch.

clue.text: Doctor in Eastern state briefly put on board

indicators.note: in places the doctor inside the other pieces

parts.note: Ark. is the short form of Arkansas
MB is a medical degree, Bachelor of Medicine

explanation.surface: A doctor in an eastern state boarding a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: To load people or cargo onto a ship is to take them aboard.

clue.text: Determine how many years in part of UK

parts.note: to determine how many is to count

explanation.surface: Working out how many years have passed in some part of Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain is divided into administrative shires, each one a region of the realm.

clue.text: Coffees with no cream, as I originally ordered

indicators.note: the letters are put in a new order, as in an order placed at a café

explanation.surface: A café customer recalling ordering black coffees, no cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso diluted with hot water; the drinks are named after American servicemen's taste.

clue.text: Kind of whisky that fly-by-nights take?

definitions.meaning: American slang for cheap, raw whiskey
a night flight that people travelling overnight board

explanation.surface: Asking what whisky a dodgy fly-by-night type drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: A fly-by-night is a shady trader, but here it is someone who literally flies by night.
explanation.definitionFit: American slang both for rotgut liquor and for an overnight passenger flight.

clue.text: Person making big hit, so to speak, in English sport

indicators.note: so to speak says the word is taken by how it is pronounced

parts.note: someone who socks, or punches hard, is a socker

explanation.surface: A batter with a huge hit in some English game.
explanation.walkthrough: The game Britons call football; Americans use the other name.
explanation.definitionFit: Association football, the game invented in England, under its American name.

clue.text: Lass hiding nothing one's put inside here

indicators.note: hiding means the girl conceals the zero within her

parts.note: a lass is a girl, a gal
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A girl with nothing to hide who ends up locked away.
explanation.walkthrough: The British spelling of a prison; 'put inside' is slang for locking up.
explanation.definitionFit: A prison is where convicts are locked up, put inside.

clue.text: Posse — it goes East, then West, to get these outlaws

parts.note: a posse is a band of people
taken as written

indicators.note: in an across clue, going West means reading right to left, so the word is written backwards

explanation.surface: A sheriff's posse riding east and then west in pursuit of bandits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it goes East' writes IT normally, then 'West' writes it backwards, TI.
explanation.definitionFit: The old Italian plural for brigands or highwaymen.

clue.text: Status of US historically terminated, coming to pass on 4th of July

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass

indicators.note: 4th of picks the fourth letter of the word July

explanation.surface: American dependency ending on Independence Day, the 4th of July.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4th of July suggests 1776, but it only gives a letter of July.
explanation.definitionFit: Before 1776 America was ruled by Britain as a dependent territory, a status that ended.

clue.text: Accessory for device in Floridian's island home

parts.note: the Florida Keys are low islands, each called a key
a pad is slang for a home

explanation.surface: A gadget accessory kept in a Florida island home.
explanation.definitionFit: A small panel of buttons attached to a gadget for entering numbers.

clue.text: Less than noble Brits initially gained admission

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of gained

parts.note: admission and entry are synonyms

explanation.surface: Not-quite-aristocratic Britons getting in somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The well-born class just below the nobility in Britain.
